# Introduction & Historical Context

## Evolution of Liver Transplantation

- **First human orthotopic liver transplant**: Starzl, 1963
- First two decades: small numbers, moribund patients, disappointing survival
- Improvements driven by:
  - Increasing surgeon experience and confidence
  - Better anesthesia
  - Improved microbiologic and immunologic treatments
  - Better immunosuppressive agents
- Currently >7,000 procedures annually in Europe and US
- Many centers report **1-year survival >90%** in elective patients

## The Donor Shortage Crisis

- Success and reduced contraindications → increasing potential recipients
- Donor numbers static or falling in many countries
- Consequences:
  - Increasing mortality on waiting list
  - Longer waits → sicker patients
  - Decreased chance of survival
  - Increased resource utilization

  
  
## The Donor Shortage Crisis

- Strategies to increase donor pool:
  - Split livers
  - Donation after circulatory death (DCD)
  - Higher risk profile donors
  - Living donors
  - Machine perfusion (evaluate and improve graft function)

## Allocation Principles

- Different healthcare systems balance:
  - **Equity**
  - **Utility**
  - **Need**
  - **Benefit**
- **North America & many European countries**: allocation based on **need**
  - Focus on reducing death on waiting list
  - Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (**MELD**) score
  
  
## Allocation Principles

- Result: reduced waiting-list mortality without appreciable effect on post-transplant survival
- Increasingly allocated by **benefit** (estimated difference in survival with/without transplant)
- **Quality of life (QOL)** increasingly considered
- Need to define **futility** — when transplantation is futile
- Palliative care must be an option

## Living Donor Liver Transplantation

- Stimulated by deceased donor shortage
- **Limitations**: risks to donor
  - Donor death risk: ~1 in 250 (depends on lobe removed)
  - Morbidity: ~30%
  - Lack of obligatory reporting and national registries → difficult to assess true risk
- Indications generally mirror deceased donation
- Some centers expanding indications (especially liver cancer, acute liver failure)

# General Indications & Contraindications

## Two Broad Indications for Grafting

1. **Survival benefit** from transplant (compared with non-transplant)
2. **QOL** (because of liver disease) unacceptable to the patient

- Where organs allocated solely on need (e.g., intractable symptoms), very long wait unless living donor access

## When to Consider Transplantation

- MELD score >17
- Signs of decompensation:
  - Ascites
  - Encephalopathy
  - Renal impairment
- Liver cell cancer for which other measures less effective
- Hepatopulmonary or portal pulmonary hypertension
- Intractable pruritus
- Intractable encephalopathy

::: {.callout-note}
Development of these criteria means transplantation should be **considered**, not necessarily that it is indicated.
:::

## Box: Indications for Referral in Adult Cirrhosis

**Symptoms**

- Hepatic decompensation
- Increasing ascites unresponsive to medical/diet therapy
- Recurrent variceal bleeding
- Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis


## Box: Indications for Referral in Adult Cirrhosis


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Side Effects of Liver Disease**

- Increasing osteopenia
- Hepatopulmonary syndrome
- Portopulmonary hypertension
- Intractable ascites / encephalopathy
- Development of hepatocellular carcinoma
- Muscle wasting and increasing frailty

:::
:::{.column width="50%"}

**Biochemical Markers**

- MELD Score >17
- Serum albumin <30 g/dL
- Serum bilirubin >50 μmol/L (parenchymal) or >100 μmol/L (cholestatic)
:::
:::

## Absolute Contraindications

- Not fit enough to withstand surgery (advanced cardiac/pulmonary disease)
- Unlikely to survive procedure (active sepsis)
- Survival after transplant too short to justify risks (metastatic disease)
- Postoperative QOL unacceptable (severe intractable depression)
- Surgery technically not possible (extensive venous thromboses)
- Patient does not choose to undergo operation

## Relative Contraindications

| Factor | Concern |
|--------|---------|
| **Age** | Older age = risk factor for poor outcomes (no agreed upper limit) |
| **Obesity** | BMI >40 kg/m² → poorer outcome |
| **Cholangiocarcinoma** | Only highly selected patients in agreed protocols |
| **Metastatic colon cancer** | Available in selected centers |
| **Chronic/refractory infections** | Depending on type and curability |
| **Poor social support** | Adversely impacts graft/patient survival |
| **Ongoing tobacco/illegal drug use** | Increased morbidities |
| **Active alcohol use** | Requires evaluation and abstinence |
| **Frailty** | Multidimensional predictor of poor outcomes |

## Changing Demographics (2019 US Data)

- **8,372** liver transplants from deceased donors
- **524** from living donors
- **1,179** died awaiting graft
- **1,186** removed from list (too sick)
- **12,706** awaiting transplant (as of April 2020)


## Changing Demographics (2019 US Data)

**Trends:**

- Rising: alcoholic liver disease, NAFLD
- Falling: cholestatic diseases, HCV (due to effective treatment)
- Living donors: not significant impact in Europe/North America; major in Asia
- DCD: increasing (~5% US, ~30% UK); risk of ischemic cholangiopathy
- Split livers: greatly reduced pediatric waiting list mortality

# General Considerations

## Malnutrition 

- **Malnutrition**: 
  - prevalence up to 60% in end-stage cirrhosis
  - Causes: disease itself, poor intake, dietary   restrictions, malabsorption, hyperammonemia
  - Associated with increased infection   susceptibility and poor outcomes
  - No convincing evidence that improving nutrition   alters transplant outcome, but prudent to optimize
  - Branch-chain amino acids and vitamin supplementation remain standard

## Frailty

- Strong predictor of:
  - Outcome in cirrhosis
  - Survival and QOL after transplant
  - Risk of acute cellular rejection
- Multidimensional construct: decreased physiologic reserve, increased vulnerability
- Focus largely on **physical frailty** (functional performance, capacity, disability)

## Frailty Assessment & Management

- Recommended: baseline and longitudinal assessment with standardized tool
- Tools used:
  - Charlson Frailty Index
  - Karnofsky performance scale
  - Liver Frailty Index (hand grip, balance, chair stands)
- Meta-analysis: **11 exercise types** improve:
  - VO₂ peak
  - Anaerobic threshold
  - 6-minute walk distance
  - Muscle mass/function
  - QOL
  
  
## Frailty Assessment & Management

- Greater improvements with **combination of aerobic + resistance exercises** at moderate-high intensity
- Neither malnutrition nor frailty should be absolute contraindications
- Waiting time should be used to improve both

## Obesity

- Increasingly common, especially with metabolic syndrome
- NAFLD is increasing indication for transplant
- Data conflicting due to:
  - Careful selection/assessment
  - Difficulty distinguishing obesity effects from associated diabetes, CVD, comorbidities
- Most studies: transplantation safe with **BMI up to 40 kg/m²**
- Some centers perform bariatric surgery peritransplant (timing/risks/benefits uncertain)

## Psychological Assessment

- Transplantation = major psychological stress for patient and family
- \>50% of candidates have wide range of psychological health problems
- Full psychiatric assessment increasingly common

**Risk factors for poor outcome:**

- Mood disorders
- Lack of social support
- Substance misuse
- Alcohol use


## Psychological Assessment

- Chronic poor health + subclinical encephalopathy + future uncertainties → difficult to predict outcome
- Expert multidisciplinary assessment required for psychiatric illness history
- **Noncompliance** (despite full support) leading to graft loss = acceptable exclusion criterion
- Particular issue in adolescents/early 20s; transitional clinics and technology may help

## Tobacco Use

- Associated with increased risk of:
  - Cardiovascular and lung diseases
  - Cancer (before and after transplantation)
  - Other morbidities
- Some centers withhold listing from active smokers or non-compliant nicotine withdrawal

## Illicit Drug Use

- Some centers exclude active illicit drug users or those failing withdrawal treatment
- **Marijuana and other illicit drugs**: outcomes not worse in users
- **Methadone**: well-stabilized patients should not be excluded
  - Continue stable dose
  - Good outcomes, though perioperative management may be challenging

## Age

- No agreed upper age limit
- Increasing age independently associated with mortality after transplant
- **Biologic age** has superseded chronologic age (but cannot readily be defined/quantified)
- Outcomes of carefully selected patients >70 are encouraging
- Older age remains independent predictor of survival before and after transplant

## Previous Abdominal Surgery

- Adhesions (especially with portal hypertension) add considerably to surgical difficulties
- May affect outcome, particularly if involving biliary tree surgery

## Infection

- **Active bacterial, fungal, or protozoal sepsis = absolute contraindication**
- Once appropriate therapy instituted → suitable candidate

## Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)

- Early studies: poor outcomes
- **HAART** greatly altered natural history
- Majority with HIV + end-stage liver disease have HCV coinfection
- Current HCV treatments also affected need for liver transplantation
- ~1% of recipients HIV-infected (2008–2015 data)
- Outcomes improved over time


## Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)

[**Indications becoming better defined:**]{.underline}

1. End-stage liver disease
2. Low or undetectable HIV RNA
3. No AIDS-defining complication
4. CD4 count >200

## Cardiovascular Disease: Overview

- Common in liver transplant candidates
- Important cause of perioperative and postoperative morbidity
- Causes:
  - Cardiovascular/valvular disease
  - Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy (CCM)
  - Metabolic diseases (amyloidosis, hemochromatosis)
  - Toxins (alcohol)
- Tools to assess degree of cardiac disease and define contraindications are imperfect

## Multivessel Coronary Artery Disease

- CAD present in **15%** of patients with end-stage liver disease
- Preoperative cardiovascular assessment is imprecise; no clear guidelines
- **Minimum**: echocardiography (heart muscle, valves, pulmonary hypertension)
- If ischemic heart disease suspected:
  - Stress test (dobutamine/adenosine-stimulated echocardiography)
  - Myoscintigraphy
- Significant stenosis (>70%) → consider revascularization before transplant
- Surgery risky in cirrhosis; **stenting may be preferable**
- Staged rather than simultaneous approach may be preferable

## Cirrhotic Cardiomyopathy (CCM)

- Defined as: systolic and diastolic dysfunction + electrophysiologic abnormalities
- Diagnosis: contemporary Doppler/echocardiography or quantitative MRI
- Characterized by:
  - High output state at rest
  - Impaired ability to increase contractility at stress
  - Diastolic dysfunction
  - Electromechanical abnormalities
- Often asymptomatic; dysfunction may not be apparent until peri/postoperative period
- Low peripheral resistance (splanchnic vasodilation) decreases LV afterload
- **Cardiac MRI** may help in diagnosis
- Features may improve after transplantation, but remains contributor to early death

## Respiratory Function: Overview

- **Routine screening**: chest X-ray, ECG, lung function tests, peripheral O₂ saturation
- Additional investigations:
  - Arterial blood gases (lying and standing → detect HPS)
  - On 100% oxygen → detect shunting
  - High-resolution CT
  - Contrast-enhanced echocardiography
  - Isotope-labeled macroaggregated albumin lung scan
  - Pulmonary angiography / right heart catheterization (as indicated)
- Arterial hypoxemia (SaO₂ <92% or PaO₂ <70 mmHg) in up to **70%** of patients with liver disease

## Causes of Pulmonary Abnormalities

1. Diseases **unrelated** to liver disease (e.g., smoking)
2. Effects **associated** with liver disease (e.g., α1-antitrypsin deficiency)
3. Respiratory conditions **associated** with liver disease (e.g., fibrosing alveolitis with PBC)
4. **Effects of liver disease** on respiratory function:
   - Ascites causing pleural effusion
   - Simple lung compression
5. **Hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS)**
6. **Portopulmonary hypertension (PPH)**

## Hepatopulmonary Syndrome (HPS)

- Detected in up to **one-third** of transplant candidates
- Results from **intrapulmonary microvascular dilation** in chronic liver disease/portal hypertension → arterial deoxygenation

**Diagnostic triad:**

1. Liver disease and/or portal hypertension
2. Elevated room air alveolar-arterial O₂ gradient (≥15 mmHg; ≥20 mmHg if >64 years)
3. Evidence of intrapulmonary vascular dilatations


## Hepatopulmonary Syndrome (HPS)

- **Orthodeoxia**: fall in arterial O₂ when standing
- Intrapulmonary shunting: contrast echocardiography or 99mTc-MAA lung-brain perfusion scan
- Improves after transplant in majority (may take >6 months)
- No association between HPS severity and cirrhosis severity
- **Severe HPS** (PaO₂ <50 mmHg or MAA shunt >20%) = predictor of increased mortality
- Association between HPS and CCM remains uncertain

## Portopulmonary Hypertension (PPH)

- **Diagnostic criteria:**
  - Liver disease resulting in portal hypertension
  - Mean pulmonary artery pressure (MPAP) >25 mmHg
- **Not correlated** with severity/etiology of portal hypertension
- Detected in **<10%** of transplant candidates

| Severity | MPAP | Significance |
|----------|------|--------------|
| Mild | <35 mmHg | Usually little concern |
| Moderate | >35 mmHg | Predictor of increased mortality |
| Severe | >45 mmHg | Predictor of increased mortality |


## Portopulmonary Hypertension (PPH)

- Diagnosis by exclusion (pulmonary emboli, intrinsic lung disease, left heart failure)
- Initial screening: contrast-enhanced echocardiography (estimate RVSP)
- Confirmation: right heart catheterization
  - MPAP >35 mmHg + PVR >240 dyn·s/cm⁵ + pulmonary wedge pressure <15 mmHg
- **Vasodilator therapy** if severe:
  - Endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan)
  - Phosphodiesterase type-5 inhibitors (sildenafil)
  - Prostanoids (epoprostenol)
- Transplant considered if MPAP reduced to <35 mmHg and PVR <400 dyn·s/cm⁵

## Coexisting Disease: Diabetes Mellitus

- Often found in chronic liver disease (especially HCV)
- May result from insulin intolerance of advanced liver disease → resolves after transplant
- Concerns: **microvascular complications**
- Insulin-dependent diabetes → worse outcome after transplant

**Relative contraindications:**

- Proliferative retinopathy
- Diabetic nephropathy
- Autonomic neuropathy (abnormal beat-to-beat variation on Valsalva, postural hypotension)
- Diabetic gastroparesis
- Advanced microvascular disease → risk of major autonomic disruption during procedure

## Coexisting Disease: Hyponatremia & Vascular Thromboses

**Hyponatremia**

- Common in advanced chronic liver disease
- Usually from injudicious diuretics or reduced free water clearance
- Severe hyponatremia (Na <120 mmol/L) → increased risk of **central pontine myelinolysis**
- Should be corrected before transplant:
  - Water restriction
  - Stop diuretics
  - Renal support if rapid correction needed
  - Aquaretics may be helpful


## Coexisting Disease:  Vascular Thromboses

- Not uncommon in chronic liver disease
- Causes: cirrhosis itself or underlying thrombotic tendency
  - Myeloproliferative disease (Budd-Chiari)
  - Lupus anticoagulant
  - Protein C/S deficiency
  - Impaired fibrinolysis
- Portal vein thrombosis: **no longer contraindication**
  - Inflow can be provided by superior mesenteric vein or splenic vein
- Only **extensive venous thrombosis** with impossible portal supply = contraindication

## Coexisting Disease: Renal Disease

- May result from **hepatorenal syndrome** or **intrinsic kidney damage**
- **Hepatorenal syndrome**: no structural kidney damage
  - Kidney functions normally once satisfactory liver function reestablished
  - Not absolute contraindication (though prognosis reduced with advanced renal insufficiency)
- **Advanced coexisting renal disease**: consider combined liver and kidney transplantation
- Renal function = major predictive factor for survival and risk of renal impairment post-transplant

## Combined liver and kidney transplantation 

- Considered for:
  - Liver failure + end-stage kidney disease   (excluding hepatorenal syndrome)
  - Liver failure + chronic kidney disease (GFR <30   mL/min)
  - Liver failure + chronic kidney disease with   renal histology showing >30% fibrosis or >30%   glomerulosclerosis
  - Liver failure + acute kidney injury (creatinine >2.0 mg/dL, renal support ≥8 weeks)

## Past History of Malignancy

- Relative contraindication (surgery + immunosuppression → early recurrence)
- Israel Penn Tumor Registry identified high-risk tumors


## Past History of Malignancy

| Risk Category | Tumors |
|---------------|--------|
| **Low (0–10%)** | Incidental renal tumors, lymphoma, testicular, uterine, cervical, thyroid |
| **Intermediate (11–25%)** | Uterine body, Wilms tumor, colon, breast, prostate |
| **High** | Bladder, sarcomas, melanoma, symptomatic renal carcinomas, myelomas, nonmelanoma skin cancers |


## Past History of Malignancy

- Most centers offer transplant when recurrence risk <10% at 5 years
- Colorectal (18.8%), nonmelanoma skin (23.5%), thyroid (25%), oral squamous (33%), vulvovaginal (33%), breast (33%) → generally >10% risk
- Only exceptional cases with these extrahepatic malignancies should be considered

## Bone Disease

- Many patients with chronic liver disease have bone disease
- **Osteomalacia** (vitamin D malabsorption): low prevalence, readily corrected with parenteral vitamin D
- **Osteoporosis**: much greater problem
  - Particularly female patients with chronic cholestatic disease
  - Successful transplantation halts/retards progression, may improve mineralization
- Severe osteoporosis with thoracic/lumbar vertebral collapse or fractures = rare indication

# Specific Diseases

## Fulminant Hepatic Failure (FHF)

- **Definition**: encephalopathy within 8 weeks of symptom onset in previously normal liver
- Accounts for **<5%** of liver transplants
- Severe FHF + grade IV encephalopathy → mortality ~**80%**

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Common causes:**

- Acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose
- Viral infections (hepatitis A, B, E; rarely C)
- Drug/xenobiotic toxicity (including herbal remedies)
- Wilson disease
- Liver diseases of unknown etiology
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Common causes of death:**

- Cerebral edema
- Multiorgan failure
- Sepsis (bacterial/fungal)
- Cardiac arrhythmia/arrest
- Respiratory failure
:::
:::

## FHF: Prognosis & Transplant Criteria

- Narrow window between recognizing poor survival and onset of irreversible complications
- Several prognostic models available for super-urgent transplant
- **King's College Hospital model**: validated and robust
- Contraindications: onset of irreversible complications
  - Irreversible cerebral edema (prolonged elevated ICP or fixed dilated pupils >6 hours)
  - Active sepsis

## FHF: Prognosis & Transplant Criteria

**Best guide to progression**: serial prothrombin time (PT) or factor V levels

  - Best represent synthetic function (in absence of   extraneous blood products)
  - Initial improvement followed by deterioration →   suggests sepsis (treat before transplant)
  - Patient at risk for ICP complications up to **48 hours** after successful transplant

**Clotting factors**: should not be given until transplant decision made (unless pressing clinical reasons)

## UK Super-Urgent Transplant Criteria for FHF (2020)


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="45%"}
**Category 1 — Acetaminophen Poisoning**

- pH <7.25 more than 24 hours after overdose and after fluid resuscitation

**Category 2 — Acetaminophen Poisoning**

- PT >100 sec or INR >6.5
- Serum creatinine >300 μmol/L or anuria
- Grade 3–4 encephalopathy
:::
:::{.column width="55%"}
**Category 3 — Acetaminophen Poisoning**

- Significant liver injury and coagulopathy
- Arterial lactate >5 mmol/L on admission and >4 mmol/L 24 hours later
- Clinical hepatic encephalopathy

**Category 4 — Acetaminophen Poisoning**

- Two of three Category 2 criteria + clinical deterioration
- (e.g., increased ICP, FiO₂ >50%, increasing inotropes) without clinical sepsis
:::
:::



## UK Super-Urgent Criteria: Non-Acetaminophen

**Category 5 — Favorable Etiologies**

(Acute viral hepatitis, ecstasy/cocaine-induced ALF)

- Clinical hepatic encephalopathy mandatory
- PT >100 sec or INR >6.5
- OR any three from:
  - Age >40 or <10 years
  - PT >50 sec or INR >3.5
  - Any grade encephalopathy with jaundice-to-encephalopathy time >7 days
  - Serum bilirubin >300 μmol/L

## UK Super-Urgent Criteria: Non-Acetaminophen

**Category 6 — Unfavorable Etiologies**

(Seronegative or idiosyncratic drug reactions)

- PT >100 sec or INR >6.5
- OR INR >2 after vitamin K repletion + any two from the Category 5 list

## FHF: Special Considerations

**Auxiliary / Partial Transplants**

- **APOLT** (auxiliary partial orthotopic liver transplantation)
- Allows earlier grafting as "safety net"
- If native liver recovers, donor liver can be removed or allowed to atrophy
- Patient returns to good liver function **free of immunosuppression**

**Artificial Liver Support**

- Role remains uncertain
- MARS (molecular absorbent recirculation system) may offer benefit


## FHF: Special Considerations

**Acetaminophen Overdose**

- Long history of unresponsive psychiatric disease or recurrent overdose → usually not appropriate
- Impulse overdose due to trivial problem → usually appropriate
- Overdose due to long-term social/domestic problems: patient may return to identical problems + transplant burden → grafting may not be appropriate

## Variants of Acute Liver Failure

**Subacute Liver Failure (Late-Onset Hepatic Failure)**

- Subacute illness with fluctuating encephalopathy
- Develops days or weeks after hepatitis-like illness onset
- Often middle-aged women, no obvious precipitating factors
- **Very poor prognosis without transplantation**

**Fulminant Autoimmune Hepatitis (AIH)**

- FHF + serologic markers of AIH (increased immunoglobulins, high-titer autoantibodies)
- Whether classic AIH form is unclear
- Response to corticosteroids disappointing
- **Decision to offer transplant should not be delayed**

## Metabolic Diseases

- Account for **<5%** of adult liver transplants
- In some cases, metabolic defect arises in liver → transplantation corrects defect
- Hepatocyte transplantation and auxiliary transplantation may become suitable alternatives


## Metabolic Diseases


**Liver-affected conditions:**


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- α1-Antitrypsin deficiency
- Wilson disease
- Protoporphyria
- Tyrosinosis / Tyrosinemia
- Galactosemia
- Glycogen storage disease types I and IV
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- Byler disease
- Hemochromatosis
- Cystic fibrosis
- Gaucher disease
- Urea cycle enzyme deficiencies
:::
:::


## Metabolic Diseases

**Other organs also affected:**

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Primary hyperoxaluria
- Crigler-Najjar syndrome
- Primary hypercholesterolemia
- Niemann-Pick disease
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- Sea-blue histiocyte disease
- Hemophilia A and B
- Protein C/S deficiency
:::
:::

## Metabolic Diseases: Special Notes

- Correction seen with Wilson disease or hemophilia
- Hypercholesterolemia: defect in liver, heart major organ affected
  - Some advocate liver transplant to prevent severe CAD
  - Combined heart and liver transplants if cardiac disease already present
- Hyperoxaluria: may require liver and kidney replacement
- Porphyria: indication in selected patients, but should accompany **stem cell transplant** (not cured by liver transplant alone)

## Metabolic Diseases: Special Notes

- Hemophilia: alternative therapies (factor VIII) available; transplant only with extensive liver disease
- Recurrence of metabolic disease not necessarily contraindication:
  - Genetic hemochromatosis: may recur, but organ damage preventable by early recognition/treatment
  - Erythropoietic protoporphyria: likely to recur, but morbidity delayed by cholestyramine

## Budd-Chiari Syndrome

- Role of transplantation remains uncertain
- Underlying thrombotic disorders:
  - Protein C/S deficiency
  - Factor V Leiden mutation
  - Lupus anticoagulant
  - Polycythemia
  - Myeloproliferative disorders
  
## Budd-Chiari Syndrome

- Some corrected by transplantation; others carry risk of complications (malignant transformation)
- Early anticoagulants and interventional radiology (especially **TIPS**) have changed management
- Transplantation considered only when:
  - Portal decompression failed or not feasible
  - Established liver failure

## Other Indications

- **Polycystic Liver Disease**
    - Indication in small proportion of patients
    - Considered when enlarged liver causes:
      - Severe and constant pain
      - Impact on stomach → poor nutrition
    - Generally indicated when liver reaches into     pelvis
    - Combined liver and kidney involvement → dual     transplantation

## Other Indications

- **Transthyretin Amyloidosis (ATTR)**
    - Progressive neurologic and cardiac impairment     from misfolded transthyretin deposition
    - Place in highly selected patients
    - Resected liver sometimes used in **domino     procedure**
    - Newer agents may reduce need:
      - TTR tetramer stabilizers
      - TTR silencers
      - Fibril disruptors

## Chronic Liver Disease: General Principles

- Most difficult problems regarding transplantation
- Main concern: **deciding appropriate time** to offer procedure
  - Fitter patient = greater probability of surviving
  - But if unsuccessful, life shortened
  - If offered too late, chances of success reduced
- Two major indications:
  1. Poor QOL
  2. Poor estimated length of life


## Chronic Liver Disease: General Principles

**QOL assessment challenges:**

- "Unacceptable" is subjective
- Difficult to disentangle borderline encephalopathy, depression, and disease-related tiredness
- Some patients adopt "sick role" — reluctant to abandon even after successful transplant
- **Intractable pruritus** = valid indication if all other measures unsuccessful
- **Lethargy alone** = not an indication (often fails to improve); exclude extrahepatic causes

## Chronic Liver Disease: Timing & Prognostic Models

- Most centers: appropriate when estimated life without transplant **<1 year**
- Diseases run predictable course, but threatened by unpredictable events (sepsis, variceal hemorrhage)
- **Timing remains inexact science**
- Factors predicting poor survival in cirrhosis **different** from those predicting post-transplant outcome


## Chronic Liver Disease: Timing & Prognostic Models

**Prognostic models:**

- **Child-Pugh (CP) score**: not sufficiently detailed for short-term survival estimation; semi-quantifiable parameters (ascites) limit generalization
- **MELD score**: useful marker of short-term prognosis; may be more accurate than CP
  - Variations (MELD-Na) exist, but MELD remains most used
- Data suggest transplanting patient without malignancy with MELD <12 associated with **reduction in 1-year survival** compared with continued waiting

**Functional tests** (aminopyrine breath test, galactosamine elimination clearance):

- Advocated by some, but rarely add to clinical/serologic assessment
- Now rarely used

## Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)

- Several prognostic models (static and time-dependent)
- Helpful in defining variables predicting survival with/without transplant
- Must be used with care (wide confidence intervals)


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Medical therapy:**

- **UDCA** (13–15 mg/kg/day): significant delay to transplant, especially with biochemical response
- **Obeticholic acid**: second-line, may further reduce need
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Indications for referral:**

- Decompensated cirrhosis
- MELD >15
- Total bilirubin >6 mg/dL (AASLD) or 3–5 mg/dL (EASL)
- Mayo risk score >appropriate threshold
:::
:::

## Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)

**Pruritus:**

- Mainstay: cholestyramine
- Other options: rifampicin, naltrexone, sertraline, plasmapheresis, MARS
- Usually disappears within 2–3 days after transplant

**Recurrence:**

- PBC recurs in allograft (slow rate) — should not preclude transplantation
- Extrahepatic manifestations will not be corrected

## Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)

- Accounts for ~**6%** of all transplants
- Natural history less clear and predictable than PBC
- Fluctuating course with exacerbations/remissions (spontaneous bacterial cholangitis)
- Underlying relentless progression toward liver failure
- Serum bilirubin and albumin remain useful markers
- CP and MELD as reliable as Mayo model


## Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)

**Timing challenges:**

- Worsening jaundice may respond to endoscopic therapy of dominant strictures or cholangitis treatment
- Development of cholangiocarcinoma adds further challenges

**Associated conditions:**

- Most cases associated with **inflammatory bowel disease** (usually ulcerative colitis)
- PSC + colitis → **increased risk of colonic cancer** vs. colitis alone
- Full colonoscopy recommended in all potential candidates
- Quiescent colitis: not contraindication
- Active colitis: treat before transplant
- Colectomy before/during transplant → protective effect against recurrent PSC

## PSC: Malignancy Risk & Transplant Considerations

- **Premalignant condition**
- Cholangiocarcinoma risk: up to **1.5%/year**, prevalence 6–13%, lifetime risk up to 20%
- Bile duct dysplasia may identify high-risk group (controversial)
- Difficult to distinguish sudden deterioration: cholangitis vs. natural history vs. cholangiocarcinoma

## PSC: Malignancy Risk & Transplant Considerations



[**Detection challenges:**]{.underline}

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Serum CEA: nonspecific, insensitive
- CA19-9: more helpful but not specific
- Imaging (CT, MRI, ultrasound, angiography): often unreliable
- MRCP: good visualization but no tissue sampling
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- ERCP + brushing/biopsy + FISH: high specificity, low sensitivity; risk of severe cholangitis
- Percutaneous biopsy/aspiration: positive diagnosis possible, but negative findings don't exclude cancer
:::
:::

## PSC: Malignancy Risk & Transplant Considerations

**Management principles:**

- Consider **earlier transplantation**
- Avoid biliary surgery if possible
- Known cholangiocarcinoma before transplant → generally **not considered** (survival poor)
- Very small proportion may benefit from aggressive neoadjuvant chemoradiation


## Alcoholic Liver Disease

- Selected patients are **excellent candidates**
- Increasing indication for transplantation
- Initial concerns largely **not substantiated**:
  - Continued excessive drinking
  - Poor compliance
  - Unreliable with immunosuppression
- Extrahepatic damage (heart, brain, pancreas, bone marrow) remains concern
- Survival rates similar to other patients with cirrhosis


## Alcoholic Liver Disease


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Ethical considerations:**

- Some argue self-induced injury should exclude patients given expense and limited donor supply
- Most units: **not appropriate to deny**
  - Not necessarily alcohol dependent
  - Many self-induced diseases exist
  - Public opinion increasingly supportive
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Specific factors to consider:**

- **Abstinence improves survival** even in decompensated patients
- Period of abstinence helpful to:
  - Ensure liver won't recover sufficiently to obviate need
  - Identify reason for excessive drinking
  - Initiate measures to reduce recurrence risk
- **No evidential basis for fixed period of abstinence**
:::
:::

## Alcoholic Liver Disease: Assessment

- Recommended: careful evaluation by multidisciplinary team including substance abuse experts

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Prognostic models:
  - Michigan alcoholism prognostic scale
  - High-risk alcoholism relapse
  - Alcohol Relapse Risk Assessment
  - Stanford Integrated Psychosocial Assessment for Transplantation
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Factors associated with sobriety:
    - Social integration (spouse/partner)
    - Stable home and work environment
    - Insight into disorder
    - Absence of failed rehabilitation attempts
    - Absence of preexisting psychiatric disorders
:::
:::

- Some centers require contract to agree to abstinence (no legal validity, but commits patient)

## Alcoholic Hepatitis

- Severe hepatitis: high serum bilirubin, prolonged clotting
- More difficult to define role than alcoholic liver disease
- Encephalopathy + renal failure → dismal prognosis
- Usually insufficient time for background evaluation
- Outcome after transplant usually poor
- Early corticosteroids may be effective in some


## Alcoholic Hepatitis

**Landmark study (Mathurin et al., 2011):**

- Highly selected patients with advanced disease, no response to medical therapy
- **77% survival at 6 months** (transplanted) vs. 27% (not transplanted)
- 2 of 26 transplanted patients returned to alcohol


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Selection criteria:**

- No prior alcoholic hepatitis episodes
- Lille scores >0.45 or rapid worsening despite medical therapy
- Supportive family members
- No severe coexisting conditions
- Commitment to alcohol abstinence
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Prognostic models:**

- Lille model
- Maddrey Discriminant Function
- Glasgow Alcoholic Hepatitis Score
- ABIC (age, bilirubin, INR, creatinine)
- MELD
:::
:::

## Alcoholic Hepatitis

- Boundaries slowly expanding; outcomes still relatively short term
- Greater need for multidisciplinary approach
- Advanced alcoholic cardiomyopathy or pancreatitis may preclude suitability

## Hepatitis A & E Viral Infection


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Hepatitis A (HAV)**

- Rarely indication for liver transplantation
- Indications same as for FHF
- Few patients have recurrent infection in graft (little clinical significance)
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Hepatitis E (HEV)**

- Another rare cause of FHF
- May persist after liver transplant
- Should be monitored; if persists, offer appropriate treatment
:::
:::

## Hepatitis B Viral Infection (HBV)

- Considered for transplant due to **FHF** or **chronic liver disease**
- Accounts for **<5%** of transplants

**FHF:**

- Conventional criteria apply
- Liver failure thought caused by rapid clearance of viral-infected hepatocytes
- Most patients HBV DNA negative at transplant → disease recurs less frequently


## Hepatitis B Viral Infection (HBV)

**Chronic liver disease:**

- HBV DNA positive at transplant → much more likely to have recurrence if untreated
- Recurrence associated with significantly poorer outcome
- High HBV DNA positivity before transplant → offer antiviral treatment where feasible/safe
- Effective antiviral therapy has significantly reduced need for transplantation


## Hepatitis B Viral Infection (HBV)

**Treatment:**

- Goal: achieve HBV DNA negativity
- **Nucleos(t)ide analogs**: entecavir or tenofovir recommended
  - Safe in decompensated liver disease
  - HBV-DNA negativity within 1 year in up to 75% of patients
  - Higher entecavir dose (1 mg) for decompensated cirrhosis
  - Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF): studies lacking in decompensated cirrhosis; alternative especially with renal impairment
- Pegylated interferon: **contraindicated** in decompensated liver disease
- Post-transplant: hepatitis B immune globulin + oral antivirals usually continued

**Hepatitis D coinfection:**
- Remains a challenge
- Interferon effective in some, but use in decompensated cirrhosis remains problematic

## Hepatitis C Viral Infection (HCV)

- Indications: same as those without HCV
- Impact of **direct-acting antiviral agents (DAAs)** dramatically reduced need for transplantation

**Pre-transplant:**

- HCV RNA positivity at transplant → infection of graft
- Previously: rapid onset of cirrhosis and graft failure → reduced survival
- Now: increasing numbers RNA negative at transplant → long-term survival likely similar to other causes
- Treatment ideally offered **before decompensation**
- Response to treatment in some has meant removal from transplant list


## Hepatitis C Viral Infection (HCV)

**Decompensated liver disease:**

- Protease inhibitor–containing regimens: **extreme caution** due to potential toxicity
- Options:
  - Treatment deferral to post-transplant period
  - Accept organ from deceased donor who also carries virus → increases chance of receiving graft

**Post-transplant:**

- Optimal time and regimen uncertain
  - Some: institute DAA once patient/graft stable
  - Others: await onset of early fibrosis


## Hepatitis C Viral Infection (HCV)

**Hemophilia + HCV:**

- Liver transplantation corrects hemophilia defect (not indication by itself)
- Many contracted HCV through contaminated blood products
- Adequate blood product support → no major problem
- Many patients need no support beyond 72 hours

## Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)

- May occur in noncirrhotic liver, but in Western populations usually arises in cirrhosis
- Accounts for up to **30%** of transplants

**Treatment approaches:**

- Chemotherapy, resection, TACE, ethanol injection, cryotherapy, RFA, microwave ablation, transplantation, immunotherapy
- Newer effective agents will change management algorithms


## Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)


**Key challenging questions:**

- Place of transplantation vs. alternative regimens?
- Biomarkers (AFP) indicating futility?
- Role of downstaging?
- Do number/size of tumors on imaging reflect spread?
- Pretransplant genomic/molecular/histologic markers?
- Impact of immunosuppression (especially mTORi)?

## HCC: Transplant Criteria

- For most patients, transplant offers **only prospect of long-term survival**
- Given organ shortage, guidelines needed for indications/contraindications

**Milan Criteria (EASL):**

- Single tumor <5 cm in diameter
- OR multiple tumors: no more than three, all <3 cm
- Based on retrospective analysis of only 48 patients
- Extrapolation to current practice requires caution (imaging detects more lesions)
- Size reflects likelihood of microinvasion/spread, not size per se


## HCC: Transplant Criteria


**UCSF (San Francisco) Expanded Criteria:**

- Solitary tumor ≤6.5 cm
- OR three or fewer nodules, largest ≤4.5 cm, total tumor diameter ≤8 cm

**Downstaging:**

- Patients initially outside Milan but reaching criteria after downstaging can be considered
- Those outside Milan: transplant only in context of agreed protocols

**Contraindications:**

- Vascular invasion
- Extrahepatic spread

## HCC: Evaluation & Management

**Serum AFP:**

- Moderately useful marker
- Many centers exclude if AFP >1000 ng/mL
- Rate of AFP increase may guide identification of tumors unlikely to be "cured"
- Molecular markers: not sufficiently sensitive/validated

**Imaging:**

- Multiphasic CT or MR
- Some use contrast-enhanced ultrasound


## HCC: Evaluation & Management

**Biopsy:**

- Risk of tumor seeding (~1%) along needle track
- Consider when:
  - Diagnosis uncertain from imaging/serology
  - Specimen needed for prognostic purposes
- Avoid in typical cirrhosis + space-occupying lesion + rapidly increasing AFP
- "Liquid biopsies": uncertain role

## HCC: Evaluation & Management


**Monitoring on list:**

- T1 tumor: AFP and imaging every 3 months
- T2 (Milan): bridging to transplant suggested to decrease progression/dropout
- T3: may be considered if downstaged to within Milan

**Immunosuppression:**

- mTORi (sirolimus, everolimus): limited survival benefit evidence
- May benefit small degree in selected patients

**Fibrolamellar / noncirrhotic primary liver tumors:**

- Indication if unresectable and no extrahepatic spread

## Cholangiocarcinoma

- Usually regarded as **contraindication** (high recurrence rates)
- Historical data: 1-year survival 53%, 3-year disease-free survival 13%

**Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (recent data):**

- 5-year overall survival: 21–56%
- Most underwent **Mayo Clinic protocol** (external beam + transcatheter radiation + IV 5-FU)
- **Dropout from protocol predictors:**
  - CA19-9 >500 U/mL
  - Mass >3 cm
  - Malignant brushing or biopsy
  - MELD >20


## Cholangiocarcinoma


**Meta-analysis (2020, Cambridge):**

- Unresectable perihilar cholangiocarcinoma, 20 studies
- **Without neoadjuvant therapy:**
  - 1-year OS: 71%
  - 3-year OS: 48%
  - 5-year OS: 32%
- **With neoadjuvant chemoradiation:**
  - 1-year OS: 83%
  - 3-year OS: 66%
  - 5-year OS: 65%
- Pooled recurrence at 3 years: 24% (with chemoradiation) vs. 52% (without)


## Cholangiocarcinoma

**Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (recent nonrandomized study):**

- Gemcitabine-based chemotherapy → ≥6 months radiographic response/stability → listed
- 21 referred, 12 accepted, 6 transplanted
- Overall survival: 100% at 1 year, 83.3% at 5 years
- 3 patients developed recurrent disease (median 7.6 months)

## Secondary Liver Cancers

- Generally **not indicated** for metastatic malignancy (high recurrence rate)
- **Major exceptions:**
  1. Carcinoid and other **neuroendocrine tumors**
  2. **Colorectal metastases (CRM)**

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs):**

- Long-term results sometimes good
- Rapid symptomatic relief
- Multidisciplinary approach required
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
**ENETS Guidelines for liver transplant:**

- Well-differentiated NET with Ki-67 ≤10%
- Primary tumor removed ≥6 months before transplantation
- <50% liver involvement
- OR <75% liver involvement with refractory hormonal symptoms
:::
:::

## Colorectal Metastases (CRM)

- Role unclear; a few European centers (notably Oslo) showed survival advantage



**SECA-I (earlier trial):**

- Overall survival with liver transplant: **60%**
- Risk factors for death:
  - CEA >80 mg/L
  - Progressive disease on chemotherapy
  - Largest lesion >5.5 cm
  - <2 years from primary resection to transplant

## Colorectal Metastases (CRM)

**SECA-II:**

- Inclusion:
  - Nonresectable liver-only metastases (CT/MRI/PET)
  - Interval diagnosis-to-transplant >1 year
  - ≥10% response to chemotherapy
- Median follow-up 36 months:
  - Overall survival at 3 years: **83%**
  - Disease-free survival: **35%**
- Recurrence mainly slow-growing pulmonary metastases (amenable to curative resection)
- Use largely reflects organ availability and recipient need
- Recurrence rates suggest need for better patient selection and treatment sequencing


## Pediatric Transplantation

- Medical indications essentially similar to adults
- **Additional indications:**
  - Growth retardation
  - Development of metabolic bone disease

**Most common indication:** disorders of the biliary system

- **Biliary atresia** most common
  - Portoenterostomy effective if performed early
  - After 2 months: limited chance of success
  - If bile drainage not established soon after surgery → consider transplant rather than further reconstruction attempts


## Pediatric Transplantation

**Other biliary disorders:**

- Alagille syndrome
- Byler disease
- Nonsyndromic intrahepatic biliary hypoplasia

**Metabolic disorders** (next most common):

- Wilson disease
- Tyrosinemia
- Glycogen storage disease
- Galactosemia
- Gaucher disease

# Assessment, Consent & Waiting List Management

## Assessment of Patients for Liver Transplantation

**Goals:**

1. Confirm diagnosis of liver disease
2. Assess indications for transplantation
3. Assess conditions that may preclude transplantation or add risk
4. Counsel patient and family about benefits and risks

**History, examination, histology review**

**Investigations depend on medical condition:**

- Some chronic diseases associated with extrahepatic diseases
  - PBC and AIH → thyroid disease, celiac disease, Addison disease
  - Exclude untreated myxedema (may cause lethargy, obviate need)

## Standard Pre-Transplant Workup

**Laboratory:**

- Complete blood count
- Clotting assessment
- Renal function tests
- Liver function tests
- Viral status: HAV, HBV, HCV, HIV, CMV
- Some centers screen for TB, HHV-8, other viruses

**Immunization:**

- Nonimmune patients: offer hepatitis A and B vaccines before transplant
- Live/attenuated vaccines contraindicated after transplant


## Standard Pre-Transplant Workup

**Tumor surveillance:**

- Ultrasound of liver + serum AFP (check for HCC in cirrhosis)

**Tuberculosis:**

- If possible history: determine previous infection
- Practice: isoniazid + pyridoxine for first 6 months after transplant

**Disease-specific blood tests:**

- Autoantibodies, immunoglobulins, copper studies, α1-antitrypsin phenotypes
- Crossmatching

## Cardiopulmonary & Radiologic Assessment


:::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Cardiopulmonary:**

- ECG, echocardiography, simple lung function tests
- Possible ischemic heart disease: echocardiogram, exercise ECG, thallium scanning, coronary angiography
- **Arterial blood gases**: important; if low O₂, repeat after exercise and 100% O₂
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Radiologic:**

- Chest radiograph
- Ultrasound: liver, biliary tree, pancreas, spleen, vessels
- If portal vein patency uncertain: angiography (direct, CT, or MR)
  - Also assess splenic/superior mesenteric vein patency
- Some units: CT/MRI only if malignancy suspected
:::
:::


## Cardiopulmonary & Radiologic Assessment

- **PSC-specific:**
  - Biliary tree investigation may reveal   undiagnosed cholangiocarcinoma
  - Endoscopic evaluation should be avoided (risk of   cholangitis)
  - Most PSC patients have colitis: screen for   active disease and cancer
  - Long history of pancolitis: full colonoscopy
    - Significant dysplasia → consider early   colectomy (immunosuppression increases colon   cancer risk)

## Additional Assessments

- **Psychiatric:**
  - Routine evaluation not indicated unless history may preclude rehabilitation

- **Dental:**
  - Examination usually required
  - Carious teeth usually removed before transplantation

- **Anesthesia:**
  - Routine assessment by anesthetist before transplant

## Consent

- Ensure candidate understands:
  - Benefits of transplant
  - Risks and implications
- Increasing shortage → use of increasingly marginal organs
- Patients must understand and accept risks:
  - Inadvertent transmission of infection (viral, bacterial, other)
  - Cancers, metabolic disorders, autoimmune diseases
  - Higher-risk grafts (split liver, DCD)


## Consent

- **Patient understanding of risk is variable**
  - Ensure fully informed consent via multiple   formats:
    - Oral
    - Printed
    - Electronic
  - Decision rests with patient, but include family   in discussions
    - Their cooperation and understanding essential   for rehabilitation
  - Consent obtained when listed; confirmed   immediately before transplantation

## Management of Patients Awaiting Transplantation

- **General principles:**
  - Maintain as fit as possible
  - Correct vitamin deficiency
  - High-protein, high-calorie diet
    - Encephalopathy should **not** exclude   high-protein diet
    - Use lactulose, metronidazole, rifaximin, or   neomycin to control encephalopathy
  - Activity program to maintain/improve physical   status


## Management of Patients Awaiting Transplantation

- **Immunization:**
  - Review history; offer immunization as indicated
  - Live/attenuated vaccines (contraindicated   post-transplant) should be given now
  - Hepatitis A and B vaccines for nonimmune   patients
  - Any infection rigorously sought and actively   treated

## Ascites Management

**Ascites:**

- May be indication for treatment (catabolic, risk of SBP)
- Prophylactic antibiotics: ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin/clavulanate
  - Efficacious, cost-effective, low resistance risk
- Severe ascites resistant to diet/diuretics + repeated paracentesis:
  - Role for **TIPS**
  - Uncertain role before transplant
  - Effective in reducing portal hypertension, improving ascites, reducing variceal hemorrhage risk
  - Risks: sepsis, perforation, portal vein thrombosis


## Varices Management

**Varices:**

- Grade II or III varices or prior variceal bleeding:
  - Pharmacoprophylaxis (propranolol or carvedilol)
  - Or banding program
- TIPS valuable in selected patients

## Disease-Specific Monitoring on Waiting List

- **PSC**: monitor for cholangiocarcinoma or bowel cancer
- **HCC**: review tumor burden (usually in context of other therapies)
- Time on waiting list can be used to adopt measures to reduce tumor spread and progression

## Avoiding Harmful Therapy

- **NSAIDs**: avoid (gastric hemorrhage, renal failure, fluid retention)
- **Opiates**: avoid (constipation, encephalopathy risk)
- **Sedatives**: avoid (encephalopathy risk)
- **Diuretics**: use with care; monitor renal function
  - Renal failure = poor post-transplant outcome
  - Hyponatremia = central pontine myelinolysis risk

## Substance Use & Waiting List Maintenance

**Alcohol use disorders:**

- Many centers: regular alcohol screening
  - Breath, blood, urine alcohol
  - Ethanol metabolites in hair

**Illicit drug use:**

- Similar considerations apply

**Tobacco:**

- If not contraindicated, use waiting time to support cessation

## Removing Patients from the Waiting List

- Transplant clinicians must remain in close contact with patient
- Problems detected and treated early
- As waiting time increases:
  - Patients deteriorate
  - May experience complications precluding successful outcome
  - Probability of survival may become too small
- With increasing donor shortage, consider criteria suggesting removal from list
